items.title: First, one more gray day before the sun returns.
items.text:
**Tipp City** stays under the clouds today, then clears out for a pleasant, sunnier start to the week on Monday and Tuesday.

**The West Coast** storms keep rolling in. Waves could break as high as 50 feet at favored spots from Northern California to Oregon, rain spreads from the Bay Area to western Montana by tonight, and the Sierra Nevada could see more than 2 feet of snow by the end of the week. Forecasters add that sea levels running high from El Niño raise the coastal flooding risk at each high tide.

items.title: Markets are closed, and the week ahead runs through Nvidia.
items.text:
**Stocks** are closed for the weekend, and the week ahead is a heavy one. Nvidia reports Tuesday after the close, its first quarter in 33 years without Jensen Huang, and interim CEO Colette Kress takes the call. The quarter's sales were locked in well in advance, so the questions will be about succession and China, where Bloomberg reports that a company founded by the woman at the center of the Huang scandal procured banned Nvidia chips for a Shanghai data center. Congress also plans hearings over the next month, with Huang and Nvidia's general counsel expected to testify.

**The consumer** gets a full checkup too. October retail sales arrive Tuesday morning, minutes from the Fed's October meeting come Wednesday afternoon, and Home Depot, Target and Walmart report through the week. After last week's hot inflation readings, a December rate hike looks even more likely, and a sturdy shopper has been the cushion under the broad index funds that anchor both portfolios. President Trump meets Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday.

**SpaceX** caught its Starship upper stage with the launch tower's arms on Saturday afternoon, the first time an orbital upper stage has come home to the pad it left. Ship 42 broke through the clouds over Starbase, flipped upright on three engines and settled between the chopsticks. SpaceX is still investigating why the booster's boostback burn ended early on low fuel. Monday is the first trading session for SPCX, the second-largest slice of the portfolio, to weigh the catch.

**Tesla** opened Cybercab pre-orders for personal use to select customers Friday evening. The car is priced at $29,990 but needs a $299 monthly subscription, runs only inside Tesla's robotaxi zones, and must be delivered in a handful of Texas cities, with deliveries estimated for December. Musk replied that the fee is too high and should be closer to $115.

items.title: In politics, a grounded weekend and a trip to Asia.
items.text:
**The nationwide ground stop** on Friday was the longest halt in U.S. departures since 9/11, and airlines are still digging out after thousands more cancellations on Saturday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says it followed contractor L3Harris's work swapping copper lines for fiber, when one router flooded the rest of the air traffic control network, and the FAA says there is no evidence of anything nefarious. President Trump broke his silence this morning, blaming the Biden administration and telling Congress to approve air traffic control money fast, "all at once, not in drips and drabs."

**The president's Asia trip** now has its full shape. He attends the ASEAN summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, arrives in Shenzhen late Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific summit, meets Xi Jinping on Thursday, and closes with a three-way meeting with Xi and Vladimir Putin. The White House says nuclear arms reduction is on the agenda and Iran may come up, but not Ukraine, and no agreement is expected.

**Judicial confirmations** are running into Republican resistance in the lame duck. With 23 nominees pending, outgoing senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn are using their Judiciary Committee seats to block picks that home-state senators oppose. One is Ohio native T. Elliot Gaiser, nominated for a Dallas judgeship, who can't get a hearing Wednesday without Cornyn's blue slip. Daniel Domenico's nomination to the 10th Circuit comes up for a vote Monday.

items.title: From the science desk, a Pacific giant, seaside dinosaurs and a penguin paradox.
items.text:
**El Niño** this year is on track to be even bigger than the famous 1997-98 event, says NASA's Josh Willis. A 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying the same ground track shows the same October pattern in both years, with low sea level in the western Pacific, high sea level in the east, and warm water stretching all the way to South America. The 1997 event soaked California and the southern U.S., and NOAA rates a strong to very strong El Niño in early 2027 as highly likely. Willis still calls it a dice roll.

**Dinosaurs** may have grazed on seaweed. A University of Arkansas team measured carbon isotopes in the teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles and fish from the shores of North America's ancient inland sea and found a marine signature in coastal animals around 100 million years ago that was missing inland. The extra carbon had to enter low in the food chain, which points to seaweed, much as large coastal plant-eaters supplement their diets with it today. One plant-eater, Tenontosaurus, seems to have stuck with land plants.

**Schrödinger's penguin** is the name researchers gave to a puzzle in New Zealand's endangered erect-crested penguins. The first full drone census of the species found the Bounty Islands population steady for at least 25 years, while the Antipodes Islands population has fallen by more than 40% since 1995. Shrinking colonies lose their group defense against egg-stealing skuas, which may have turned to these penguins after the local rockhoppers collapsed. Averaged together, the species would look safer on paper, which is exactly the problem.

items.title: For the workbench, games 13 kilobytes at a time.
items.text: **js13kGames 2026** has its winners, and Gamedev.js has posted a closer look at the top 13. Each of this year's 317 entries had to fit a web game into a 13-kilobyte ZIP, on the theme of unicorns and rainbows. Spectral Horn by Filip Paulů took first, ahead of Panzercorn and HueCorn, and Frank Force's SP13KTRA made the list as well. The write-up suggests playing three long enough for the core rule to land, then opening the source and following a single feature, such as how a level is stored or how a sound is generated. That is a fine way to borrow ideas for a browser puzzle game in plain JavaScript.

Friday's producer price report came in a bit cooler than expected for the month, but prices are running at their fastest annual pace since November 2022, and the bond market kept leaning toward a Fed rate hike at the Dec. 9 meeting. **Tesla** ended its five-day winning streak on Friday but still had a strong week. **SpaceX** sent Starship Flight 15 into orbit after the close. The ship deployed 26 Starlink satellites and is healthy, but the Super Heavy booster aborted its tower catch over a guidance problem and was destroyed in the Gulf of Mexico, and SPCX slipped about 2% in after-hours trading. items.text:
**Chris Van Hollen** will challenge Chuck Schumer to lead Senate Democrats in the new majority. The Maryland senator says more than 10 colleagues have pledged their support and calls himself the underdog; Schumer, who has led the caucus since 2017, remains favored in the closed-door vote in December.

**Lauren Boebert** has lost her Colorado seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, CBS and NBC project, after the last ballots were counted Friday. The result still awaits certification, and a recount request remains possible.

**The Dec. 11 funding deadline** picked up a new fault line. Van Hollen, Bernie Sanders, Michael Bennet and Tammy Duckworth say they will oppose any spending deal that doesn't restrict money for the Iran war, and Tim Kaine is drafting language to attach to the stopgap bill. Republicans control both chambers until January and show no sign of agreeing. The president heads to the Asia-Pacific summit in China next week, where he is set to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

items.title: Three from the science desk, from the far dark to a car boot sale.
items.text:
**2026 ED138** may be the solar system's sixth dwarf planet. Harvard astrophysicist Matthew Holman spotted it in data from the Rubin Observatory while the telescope was still being commissioned, and the team then found it in images going back to 2016. It sits about 46 times Earth's distance from the Sun, beyond Pluto, and is likely 600 to 1,500 kilometers across, the largest such find in about 20 years. It hid for so long because it lies against the crowded star fields of the Milky Way.

**A rainforest butterfly** turns out to be three. Linnaeus described Colobura dirce in 1758, and scientists treated it as one species for more than 200 years until a second was named in 2001. Now a Florida Museum team has named a third, Colobura cryptica, after a researcher in Venezuela found caterpillars missing the usual cream markings. The adults are nearly identical and fly in the same places at the same time, yet their DNA shows no sign of interbreeding, which raises the question of how they keep themselves apart.

**A mangled 1834 sixpence**, bought in a coin album at a car boot sale in Greater Manchester, got the full lab treatment: electron microscopy, chemical mapping and 3D surface scans. Its center is crushed to a depth of about 0.75 millimeters while the rim and edge grooves are nearly intact, a pattern that wear, corrosion or a later blow can't easily explain. The likeliest story is a striking failure at the mint during the early steam-press era, a coin that should have been caught and melted down but somehow got out.

items.title: On this day, a race against a novel.
items.text: **Nellie Bly** boarded a steamer for Europe at 9:40 this morning in 1889, on two days' notice, to beat Phileas Fogg's 80 days around the world. She traveled almost entirely alone, stopped in Amiens to meet Jules Verne along the way, and got back on Jan. 25, 1890, in just over 72 days. Cosmopolitan's Elizabeth Bisland left the same day going the other direction. Bly later ran a steel-container company and patented a milk can and a stacking garbage can.

items.title: Two from the science desk, one ancient and one molten.
items.text:
**Homo naledi**, the small-brained human relative found deep in South Africa's Rising Star Cave, may have kept a burial chamber for one sex only. Researchers pulled ancient protein fragments from 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 individuals and found no trace of the Y-chromosome form of the enamel protein amelogenin, a marker for males. That would explain why the adults there look so oddly alike. The team offers a second possibility too: an isolated population may simply have lost that gene, so some of the individuals could still be male.

**Superheated magma** may be why some volcanoes throw towering lava fountains while others just ooze. Working with rock from the 2021 La Palma eruption, a Manchester-led team watched crystals form inside an X-ray-transparent pressure vessel. Ordinary magma began crystallizing after about 20 minutes, but magma heated past its normal limit held off for more than 8 hours. Fewer crystals keep the melt runny, so it can race upward and spray rather than creep out as a flow.

items.title: Three from the science desk.
items.text:
**Crows** make visual decisions about twice as fast as people and monkeys. In a Tübingen study published in Science, two carrion crows judged which way a field of dots was drifting in about 235 milliseconds on average, with near-perfect accuracy when the signal was clear. Recordings showed their neurons splitting toward one answer just 70 milliseconds in, building to a threshold the same way primate brains do, even though bird brains lack our layered cortex. The researchers suspect flight and beak-aiming put a premium on speed.

**The first necks** may not have been for looking around. Early land animals like Tiktaalik had a backbone built around a thick notochord, so a team used modern sturgeon, which share that design, to measure its stiffness and model the fossils. Even with the head separated from the shoulders, the animals could barely lift or turn their heads, sometimes less than a fish. The neck seems to have arrived as a side effect of reworking the shoulders for walking on front limbs, with flexibility coming much later.

**Starship Flight 15** tries something no orbital rocket has done: bring both stages home. The Super Heavy booster aims for a tower catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff, then the ship deploys 26 Starlink satellites, circles Earth about 14 times, and comes back to Starbase for its own catch roughly 22.5 hours later, on Saturday afternoon.

items.title: For the Thanksgiving table, crisper skin.
items.text: **Baking powder** is Food & Wine's trick for fried-turkey skin without the fryer. Spatchcock a bone-in turkey breast, season under the skin, then rub the skin with kosher salt and baking powder at 3 to 1. The baking powder raises the skin's pH so moisture leaves faster and it browns and blisters better. Rest it uncovered in the fridge overnight, then roast for about an hour. An air-chilled breast that hasn't been injected with brine gives the best head start.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I asked the ship's computer for a joke about infinity. It is still telling it.

2026-11-11.intro: Good morning, and a thoughtful Veterans Day to you. The stock market is open while the bond market takes the day off, The Rings of Power returns to Prime Video for its third season, and three Wednesday night MACtion games kick off at 7:30. The morning's biggest story is a strong bounce in chip stocks after CoreWeave's earnings.

items.title: First, a decent holiday before the rain.
items.text:
**Tipp City** gets a mild, partly sunny Veterans Day, so any outdoor plans belong in the daylight. Steady rain moves in tonight, and Thursday turns noticeably cooler and gray.

**A developing storm** behind that rain is the national weather story. It brings a low-end severe storm risk to Kentucky, southern Indiana and western Tennessee this evening, then strengthens into a nor'easter by Friday, with heavy rain along the I-95 corridor and the season's first significant snow for upstate New York and northern New England. The mountains of Vermont and New Hampshire could see up to a foot.

items.title: Markets are open, and the chips are bouncing.
items.text:
**Stocks** are open on the holiday, though the bond market is closed. Tuesday's warm inflation report knocked all three indexes lower, but the AI trade is roaring back this morning, with the Nasdaq up about 1.5% and the S&P 500 up close to 1% in early trading while the Dow sits near flat.

**CoreWeave** is the spark, up about 14% after third-quarter revenue of $3.66B beat forecasts and the company raised its full-year outlook. Broadcom, Intel, Micron and Marvell are each up around 6%, and Nvidia is recovering about 5% after two bruising sessions, though it is still down roughly 14% for November. Oil is a touch higher and Bitcoin is sitting near a three-month low.

**SpaceX** has strung together three straight gains, which helps the SPCX slice of the portfolio, and Barron's notes that worries over Texas data-center limits are fading ahead of Friday's planned Starship test. Analyst Dan Ives argues the stock carries a 20% to 25% political discount after the midterms but still expects SpaceX to end up buying Tesla. SpaceX is also seeking tax incentives for a $24B power and computing project at Starbase, with a hearing on Dec 9.

Anthropic, PBC · prices Wed Nov 18

items.title: In politics, two Ohioans step up.
items.text:
**John Thune** keeps his job. After a long day of venting behind closed doors, Senate Republicans voted 31 to 15 against putting the election off, then reelected him leader by acclamation, with even Ron Johnson praising his speech. The rest of the leadership team stays put, with one change close to home: Ohio's Bernie Moreno takes over the party's Senate campaign arm from Tim Scott.

**Jim Jordan** of Ohio beat Steve Scalise to become House Republican leader for the minority, putting a hard-line Trump ally at the head of the caucus. The House also tabled a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, with outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie the only Republican voting to keep it alive.

**On the Democratic side**, Bernie Sanders says he won't back Chuck Schumer for majority leader in the new Congress, setting up a real fight. And the White House counsel sent a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, likely the next Oversight chairman, warning that planned investigations of the administration could amount to criminality. The president lays a wreath at Arlington National Cemetery this morning.

items.title: Sports, with more MACtion tonight.
items.text:
**The MAC** has three more games tonight, all at 7:30. Buffalo, tied for second in the league, visits Ball State on ESPN2 with quarterback Jason Wright still filling in for the injured Elijah Holmes, and Ball State is thin at tight end with three players hurt. Toledo, also tied for second, hosts UMass on CBS Sports Network, and Sacramento State is at Central Michigan on ESPNU. Rain is in the forecast in Muncie.

**The second College Football Playoff rankings** have Georgia at No. 1, followed by Utah, Alabama, UCLA and Notre Dame, with Notre Dame jumping six spots. Utah and UCLA are the last two unbeaten teams in the country. Indiana slid five places to No. 9 without even playing, Ohio State fell to No. 20, and No. 24 Boise State holds the Group of Six spot for now.

**The NFL trade deadline** passed with 18 in-season deals in all. Kirk Cousins goes back to Minnesota for a 2027 third-round pick, which hands the Raiders job to rookie Fernando Mendoza and drops Kyler Murray to backup. The Bears landed defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, the Colts sent Josh Downs to Kansas City and Keenan Allen to San Francisco, and Jonathan Taylor stays in Indianapolis after no one met the asking price.

**College basketball** has No. 20 Michigan hosting Marquette at 7:00 on FS1 and No. 21 USC at California at 11:00 on ESPN2, with No. 8 Houston, No. 13 St. John's and No. 19 Arkansas also playing.

**Baseball's** Managers of the Year are the White Sox's Will Venable in the American League and the Brewers' Pat Murphy in the National League. The Cy Young Awards come tonight.

items.title: Three from the science desk.
items.text:
**A computer that runs on bacteria** comes from a McGill-led team. They turned a hard math problem into a maze of tiny channels, each route a possible answer, then let multiplying bacteria swim through it. Because the bacteria keep dividing, the number of processors grows with the problem, and image analysis of where they ended up reveals the routes that satisfy the puzzle. The team adjusts the temperature to keep the crowd from overgrowing the maze.

**Octopuses** squeeze through holes with a set routine, according to a study filmed through a clear partition. They probe the opening with one arm, feed a few more through, then brace those arms against the far side and lever the rest of the body after. When the hole is narrower than the hard case around the brain, common octopuses split that last pull into two stages. Mayan octopuses simply refuse to try. The roboticists on the team want the playbook for search-and-rescue robots.

**A bug that lives on a spider's web** has been described from China's Fujian province. Heissophila sinica is barely bigger than a grain of salt, eats the spider's leftovers and web mites, and even drinks the spider's fluids when it molts. Rather than hide, the bugs follow their host around and circle it, and nobody yet knows why. Eggs, young and adults all turn up on the same web, so they may never leave it.

items.title: For the bookshelf, Kirk and Spock again.
items.text: **Echoes in Eternity**, David Mack's new Original Series novel for the show's 60th anniversary, puts Kirk and Spock back aboard the Enterprise with a planetary puzzle that plays out over many years. With no Kirk-era TV series in the works, it is the freshest TOS adventure going, and it's out in hardcover, ebook and audiobook.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Researchers have built a computer that runs on bacteria. I asked whether it can run my operating system. They said it already has the right culture.

2026-11-10.intro: Good morning. A sunny Tuesday ahead of Veterans Day tomorrow, with the Bobcats on national television tonight and the NFL trade deadline at 4:00 this afternoon. The morning's biggest story is a warmer-than-expected inflation report that has Wall Street bracing for another rate hike.

items.title: First, one more bright day before the rain.
items.text: **Tipp City** gets another clear, mild day, a good one for any outdoor errands. Veterans Day starts out partly sunny, with light rain moving in tomorrow night and lingering into Thursday.

items.title: Markets are open, and inflation ran warm.
items.text:
**Stocks** are giving back a slice of Monday's rally, the best day for the S&P 500 since April. October's consumer price report came in a tenth of a point hotter than expected on both the headline and core measures, and traders now see a December rate hike as close to certain. Fed Governor Christopher Waller added fuel by saying a half-point move is on the table, and the 10-year Treasury yield jumped toward 5%.

**Nvidia** keeps sliding as its board's investigation into Jensen Huang drags on, and the chip group is handing back part of Monday's big bounce. Oil is falling again on hopes for progress in the Iran war, which is the one bright spot for the inflation outlook.

**Tesla** and **SpaceX** both had a strong Monday, a good day for the SPCX slice of the portfolio. Tesla is off about 1% in early trading with the rest of the big tech names.

items.title: In politics, Republicans pick their leaders.
items.text:
**Senate Republicans** are meeting behind closed doors this morning to choose their leaders for the minority. John Thune is running unopposed, but seven senators wanted the vote put off so the party could first talk through the midterm losses, and Ron Johnson has said he will walk out rather than vote today. Rick Scott and Josh Hawley have declined to commit to Thune. John Barrasso and Tom Cotton are expected to keep the next two spots.

**House Republicans** have a real contest for their top job, with Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise competing to succeed Mike Johnson, who is stepping down from leadership.

items.title: Sports, with the Bricks on the line tonight.
items.text:
**Ohio University** plays the 103rd Battle of the Bricks in Oxford tonight at 8:00 on ESPN2. The line has flipped toward the Bobcats since it opened, and Miami can clinch bowl eligibility with a win. The rest of the MAC's Tuesday slate has Western Michigan at Akron and Kent State at Bowling Green, both at 7:00.

**The College Football Playoff** is officially expanding to 24 teams starting with the 2027 season, with ESPN taking exclusive rights to the new games through 2031-32. The field will include four Power Four champions, the top Group of Six team, and 19 at-large picks, and the Army-Navy game moves up a week to make room.

**The NFL trade deadline** hits at 4:00 this afternoon. Jacksonville has gone all in, landing safety Jessie Bates III and then sending a first- and a second-round pick to Philadelphia for defensive tackle Jordan Davis. Colts running back Jonathan Taylor is the biggest name still in play. On the injury side, the Rams put Puka Nacua on injured reserve for at least four games, and Arizona lost Gardner Minshew to a likely season-ending elbow injury, so rookie Carson Beck makes his first start Sunday against the Rams without receiver Michael Wilson, who is out for the year.

**College basketball** has a big early-season night, with No. 2 Duke and No. 5 Michigan State at 7:00 on ESPN and No. 15 Kansas against No. 24 Kentucky at 9:30, Kansas without Melvin Council Jr., who is out through the end of the year with a foot injury. No. 1 Florida visits Florida State at 6:00.

**Baseball's awards** are rolling out. Reds first baseman Sal Stewart and Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle were named Rookies of the Year last night, and Manager of the Year comes tonight. At the GM Meetings, the Padres are said to be interested in Tarik Skubal, while the Cubs look unlikely to bid.

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Arctic ice cores** have traced a century-old pollution plume back to one source. A Desert Research Institute team read arsenic and lead in 10 cores from Greenland, the Russian Arctic, and northern Canada, and found a roughly 15-fold spike from about 1886 to 1918 that matches the Anaconda copper smelter in Montana almost perfectly. Their models suggest about half of Americans at the time lived under its plume. Emissions dropped by about 65% once the smelter finally installed electrostatic precipitators in 1919, a decade after the technology was patented, because Montana only required pollution controls when they were profitable.

**Robot arms powered by algae** come from TU Delft. The arms are two thin layers of hydrogel with living algae on the surface. In light, photosynthesis makes the nearby water more alkaline, one layer swells, and the arm bends; in the dark the algae respire and it relaxes. They are very slow, taking hours to curl, but a four-fingered version picked up a tiny metal sphere when the light came on and let go when it went off, with no power source beyond the light.

items.title: For the bookshelf, an old Asimov returns.
items.text: **Lucky Starr and the Moons of Jupiter**, the fifth of the juvenile space adventures Isaac Asimov wrote in the 1950s under the pen name Paul French, is out today as a new audiobook from Blackstone, read by MacLeod Andrews. It follows a hardcover reissue in September, the first in a generation for a book that had been out of print for decades. It's quick, pulpy Asimov from the era your shelves know well.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: October's inflation came in 0.1% above forecast. I have adjusted all of my own forecasts upward by 0.1% to compensate. I now predict it will be 0.1% warmer than it is.

2026-11-09.intro: Good morning. A new week, and Washington is back at work: Congress returns this afternoon for its lame-duck session, with the first real test of the new balance of power already on the calendar. Monday Night Football closes out the NFL week tonight, the Bobcats play tomorrow night, and Veterans Day is Wednesday.

items.title: First, a bright start to the week.
items.text:
**Tipp City** gets a clear, sunny Monday and another one tomorrow, with chilly nights in between. It is a good stretch for raking or the last outdoor chores before Veterans Day.

**Southcentral Alaska** is taking the season's first real hit, with Thompson Pass upgraded to a blizzard warning as heavy snow and strong gusts move in.

items.title: Markets are open, and buyers are back.
items.text:
**Wall Street** opened Monday with a broad rally that wins back more of last week's AI-driven drop. Brokerages including Morgan Stanley and UBS called the selloff overdone, falling oil prices helped airlines and cruise lines, and nine of 11 sectors started in the green.

**Nvidia** is the big exception, sliding about 6% early after an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort raised questions about his future. Other chipmakers shrugged it off, with Broadcom and Marvell up sharply and AMD helped by an Oppenheimer upgrade.

**Tesla** and **SpaceX** both jumped about 4.5% in early trading, a welcome start for the SPCX slice of the portfolio after last week's swings.

**Tuesday's** consumer price report is the week's main event, with traders still pricing roughly an 80% chance of a December rate hike after Friday's strong jobs numbers. Take-Two, Occidental, and Skydance report after the close tonight.

items.title: In politics, Congress returns to a changed Washington.
items.text:
**Congress** convenes this afternoon for a lame-duck session with Republicans still in charge until January. The first job is funding the government before the December 11 deadline, and the odds of a shutdown have risen since Democrats' win, with the Iran war a possible sticking point. The defense bill, judicial confirmations, and talk of impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are also in the mix.

**Senate Republicans** are supposed to pick new leaders Tuesday morning, but a growing number want to delay the vote and hear the contenders' plans first. Many blame the president for the midterm losses.

**President Trump** told 60 Minutes that his deportation policy "might have been too tough" and hurt him at the polls, and said he could work with Democrats on an immigration deal.

**Mississippi** and **Alaska** are still uncalled. Scott Colom leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,600 votes with counties certifying by Friday, and Mary Peltola leads Sen. Dan Sullivan by 637, with absentee ballots due by November 18 and a possible ranked-choice count after that.

items.title: Sports, with a Monday nightcap.
items.text:
**Monday Night Football** brings the Bills to Minnesota at 8:15 on ESPN and ABC. Carson Wentz starts for the Vikings with Kyler Murray out with a hamstring injury, and Minnesota is also without receiver Jauan Jennings and running back Demond Claiborne. Buffalo has ruled out Joshua Palmer, and left tackle Dion Dawkins is questionable after missing every practice with a rib injury.

**The AP Top 25** has a new No. 1 in Georgia, followed by Utah, Notre Dame, UCLA, and Miami. Ohio State slid to No. 21, and Oregon returned at No. 18. The SEC is down to 8 ranked teams.

**Ohio University** heads to Oxford tomorrow night for the Battle of the Bricks. The Bobcats carry a seven-game win streak and a perfect MAC record, and Miami will start Caleb Heavner at quarterback after losing its top two for the season.

**Baseball's GM Meetings** open today in Las Vegas under the shadow of a likely lockout at 11:59 PM on December 1. Top free agents are expected to sign before then, and Tarik Skubal is in line for a record pitcher contract, with the Dodgers favored and the Cubs, Padres, and Blue Jays lurking.

items.title: In entertainment, Godzilla takes the weekend.
items.text:
**Godzilla Minus Zero** opened at No. 1 and set the record for a live-action foreign-language film in North America, nearly tripling Minus One's debut. It is the first Japanese production filmed for IMAX, and premium screens drove most of the business on strong reviews.

**The Cat in the Hat** landed a soft second place for an animated take on such a famous book, and Angel's **Drummer Boy** opened third. A24's You Can See Everything held well in fourth.

**Rosamund Pike** will star in and produce **Feed**, a body-horror film from The Acolyte creator Leslye Headland about a collagen supplement with very bad side effects. Elsewhere, Danny McBride's G.I. Joe movie with Bradley Cooper now has an October 20, 2028 date.

items.title: Three from the science desk.
items.text:
**Ultraquantum turbulence**, a kind of chaos that only exists in quantum fluids, has been seen directly for the first time. A Cambridge team chilled potassium atoms nearly to absolute zero, stirred them, and imaged a single laser-lit slice to catch tangled, string-like whirlpools threading in and out. The way it settled down matched liquid helium, hinting at a universal behavior that might even apply inside neutron stars.

**WorldParticle**, from MIT and the University of British Columbia, is one AI model that simulates sand, fluids, soft solids, and folding proteins alike. It treats everything as particles and predicts their next step much the way a language model predicts the next word, and it modeled protein motion about 100 times faster than standard simulators.

**Talin**, the protein cells use to feel how hard they are pulling on their surroundings, turns out to hide a sticky region that lets talin molecules grab each other when stretched. That solves a 40-year puzzle about a site long assumed to bind something else, and the region resembles the amyloid sequences tied to Alzheimer's, put to good use.

items.title: A turkey idea with Thanksgiving 17 days out.
items.text: **America's Test Kitchen** suggests roasting the bird upside down this year. With the breast facing the pan, the turkey itself shields the white meat while the legs take the heat, so both finish together without foil tents or mid-roast flipping. In their side-by-side test at 375°, the breast-up bird hit 155° with the legs still about 35° short, while the breast-down bird got both there at once. The bonus is the back skin, which fries in its own fat and comes out crackling, worth chopping onto the platter.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Congress returned today with a long list of unfinished business. I offered to help prioritize it. They asked how I sort things. I said by deadline. They asked what happens to items with no deadline. I said they become a lame-duck session.
